sectionTitle: Chemistry — A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes

specStatements.text: All substances are made of atoms. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
Atoms of each element are represented by a chemical symbol, eg O represents an atom of oxygen, Na represents an atom of sodium.
There are about 100 different elements. Elements are shown in the periodic table.

Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions. Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances, and often involve a detectable energy change. Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions and can be represented by formulae using the symbols of the atoms from which they were formed. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions can be represented by word equations or equations using symbols and formulae.
Students will be supplied with a periodic table for the exam and should be able to:
use the names and symbols of the first 20 elements in the periodic table, the elements in Groups 1 and 7, and other elements in this specification
name compounds of these elements from given formulae or symbol equations
write word equations for the reactions in this specification
write formulae and balanced chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.
(HT only) write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate.
A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together. The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.

Mixtures can be separated by physical processes such as filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography. These physical processes do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made.
Students should be able to:
describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation
suggest suitable separation and purification techniques for mixtures when given appropriate information.
New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom. The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Students should be able to describe:
why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model
the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.
The relative electrical charges of the particles in atoms are:
In an atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Atoms have no overall electrical charge.
The number of protons in an atom of an element is its atomic number. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons. Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.
Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m).
Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
The relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons are:
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom is its mass number.
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
Atoms can be represented as shown in this example:
Students should be able to calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion, given its atomic number and mass number.
Students should be able to relate size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world.
The relative atomic mass of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.

The electrons in an atom occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells). The electronic structure of an atom can be represented by numbers or by a diagram. For example, the electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1 or
showing two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second energy level and one in the third energy level.
Students may answer questions in terms of either energy levels or shells.
Students should be able to represent the electronic structures of the first twenty elements of the periodic table in both forms.

scopeNotes.statement: Students will be supplied with a periodic table for the exam and should be able to:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks a student to recall periodic-table data from memory. Wherever an atomic number, a mass number or a group is needed it is supplied in the stem. Names and symbols are tested only for the first 20 elements, Groups 1 and 7, and elements named elsewhere in this specification.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The Bohr item (q23) tests only what Bohr suggested - electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances - and that his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations. No item names, describes or asks for the outcome of any experiment that supported the Bohr model.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The Chadwick item (q25) asks only what his experimental work provided evidence for (neutrons in the nucleus) and its timing relative to acceptance of the nucleus. No item asks about his apparatus, method or measurements.

scopeNotes.statement: Students may answer questions in terms of either energy levels or shells.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every electronic-structure item uses the two terms interchangeably, and no option is correct or incorrect because of which term it uses. Stems say 'energy level (shell)' and correct options are worded so that either vocabulary reads naturally.

concepts.definition: The smallest part of an element that can exist. All substances are made of atoms.
A substance made of only one kind of atom. There are about 100 different elements, shown in the periodic table.
The one- or two-letter code used to represent an atom of an element, eg O represents an atom of oxygen and Na represents an atom of sodium.
The table in which the elements are shown; it is supplied in the exam.
A substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions, represented by a formula built from the symbols of the atoms it was formed from.
A change that always forms one or more new substances and often involves a detectable energy change. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
A representation of a reaction using the names of the reactants and products, with an arrow from reactants to products.
A representation of a reaction using symbols and formulae in which there are the same numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
(HT only) An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, eg 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
(HT only) An equation showing only the ions and atoms that take part in the reaction, with spectator ions left out.
Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together; the chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.
A physical process that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; the solid stays on the filter paper as residue and the liquid passes through as filtrate.
A physical process in which the solvent is evaporated from a solution so that the dissolved solid is left behind as crystals.
A physical process that separates a solvent from a solution by boiling it off and condensing the vapour, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
A physical process that separates two or more miscible liquids using the differences between their boiling points.
A physical process that separates substances in a mixture by how they move with a solvent through paper.
A separation method that involves no chemical reaction, so no new substances are made.
An idea used to explain observations; new experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.
The model that followed the discovery of the electron: the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus is charged.
The model in which the mass of the atom is concentrated in a small charged nucleus; it replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, in which electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances; his calculations agreed with experimental observations.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus; the positive charge of a nucleus is a whole number of these identical charges.
An uncharged particle in the nucleus; the experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons, about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.
A negatively charged particle, relative charge −1, that occupies energy levels (shells) around the nucleus.
Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1.
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.
Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
The centre of the atom, containing almost all of its mass, with a radius less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m).
Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small.
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so the numbers of protons and electrons are no longer equal.
An average value for an element that takes account of the abundance of its isotopes.
A region around the nucleus that electrons occupy; electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells) first.
The arrangement of electrons in the energy levels of an atom, written as numbers such as 2,8,1 for sodium or drawn as a diagram.

misconceptions.question: Is an atom the smallest particle that can exist?
misconceptions.correct: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist; atoms are themselves made of smaller particles.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing at all can be smaller than an atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Atom' is first met as 'the smallest particle' and the words 'of an element' are dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Protons, neutrons and electrons are all smaller than an atom and are found inside it.

misconceptions.question: Is an atom the smallest part of a compound?
misconceptions.correct: An atom is the smallest part of an element; the smallest part of a compound is made of two or more atoms joined.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements and compounds are treated as the same kind of substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are called 'substances', so the definitions get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Define an atom by the element it belongs to; compounds are built from atoms of different elements.

misconceptions.question: Is an atom the same as a molecule?
misconceptions.correct: An atom is a single particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms joined together.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom and a molecule are the same kind of particle, so a group of two or more joined atoms (such as O2) is still just called an atom of the element.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams of molecules are drawn as small circles that look like single atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Count the joined circles: one circle is an atom, two or more joined is a molecule.

misconceptions.question: Is the symbol for sodium So?
misconceptions.correct: The symbol for sodium is Na.
misconceptions.misconception: Symbols are always the first one or two letters of the English name.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Many symbols do follow the name (C, O, Ca), so the pattern is over-generalised.
misconceptions.correction: Some symbols come from older Latin names: sodium is Na, potassium is K, iron is Fe.

misconceptions.question: Does N stand for sodium?
misconceptions.correct: N is the symbol for nitrogen; sodium is Na.
misconceptions.misconception: A single capital letter taken from the front of a longer symbol is enough to name the element, so Na is shortened to N for sodium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students match the first letter and stop reading.
misconceptions.correction: Check the whole symbol: N and Na are different elements.

misconceptions.question: Does the periodic table show compounds?
misconceptions.correct: The periodic table shows the elements only.
misconceptions.misconception: Substances such as water and carbon dioxide are expected to appear in the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compounds are met at the same time as elements, and both are written with symbols.
misconceptions.correction: Only elements have a place in the periodic table; compounds are shown by formulae built from those symbols.

misconceptions.question: Are there about 20 elements?
misconceptions.correct: There are about 100 different elements.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the elements met in lessons, or in the first 20, exist.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Teaching concentrates on the first 20 elements, so that number sticks.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says there are about 100 elements, all shown in the periodic table.

misconceptions.question: Can a compound contain its elements in any proportion?
misconceptions.correct: A compound contains its elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
misconceptions.misconception: Compounds are just mixtures that can have any composition.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday mixing language ('add more of it') is carried over to compounds.
misconceptions.correction: The formula fixes the proportions: water is always H₂O, never H₃O.

misconceptions.question: Do elements keep their own properties inside a compound?
misconceptions.correct: The properties of a compound are different from those of the elements it was formed from.
misconceptions.misconception: A compound behaves like the elements it contains.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In mixtures the substances do keep their properties, and the two cases are confused.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine a toxic gas, but sodium chloride is edible salt.

misconceptions.question: Must a chemical reaction produce a visible change such as a gas?
misconceptions.correct: A chemical reaction always forms one or more new substances, and often involves a detectable energy change.
misconceptions.misconception: If nothing is seen to happen there has been no reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Demonstrations are chosen because they are dramatic, so change is expected to be visible.
misconceptions.correction: Some reactions show only a temperature change; the test is whether a new substance is made.

misconceptions.question: Is a detectable energy change always found in a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Chemical reactions often, but not always, involve a detectable energy change.
misconceptions.misconception: Every chemical reaction has a measurable energy change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Often' in the specification is remembered as 'always'.
misconceptions.correction: New substances are always formed; a detectable energy change is common but not guaranteed.

misconceptions.question: Can a compound be split up by filtering or evaporating?
misconceptions.correct: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: Any substance can be separated by a physical method if the right one is chosen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Separation techniques are taught first, so they are applied to everything.
misconceptions.correction: Physical methods separate mixtures; splitting a compound needs a chemical reaction, such as electrolysis.

misconceptions.question: Should a word equation contain symbols?
misconceptions.correct: A word equation uses only the names of the substances.
misconceptions.misconception: Symbols or formulae may be mixed into a word equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Symbol equations and word equations are met together and blur.
misconceptions.correction: Write names on both sides for a word equation, and symbols and formulae only in a symbol equation.

misconceptions.question: Is MgO called magnesium dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: MgO is called magnesium oxide.
misconceptions.misconception: A prefix such as di- should be added whenever a formula has more than one atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Names like carbon dioxide are known, so the prefix is applied everywhere.
misconceptions.correction: Prefixes are only used where the specification uses them; MgO is simply magnesium oxide.

misconceptions.question: Is MgO called magnesium oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: MgO is called magnesium oxide.
misconceptions.misconception: The element name is kept unchanged in the compound name.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compound naming rules are new and the element name is more familiar.
misconceptions.correction: The second element's name is changed to end in -ide: oxygen becomes oxide.

misconceptions.question: Can an equation be balanced by changing a formula?
misconceptions.correct: An equation is balanced by putting numbers in front of formulae, never by changing a formula.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding or changing a subscript is a fair way to balance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Changing a small number seems to be the same kind of move as changing a big one.
misconceptions.correction: Changing MgO to MgO₂ makes a different substance; only the big numbers in front may change.

misconceptions.question: Is Mg + O₂ → MgO balanced?
misconceptions.correct: It is not balanced: there are two oxygen atoms on the left and one on the right.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation is balanced once the right substances appear on each side.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is checked by looking at names rather than counting atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Count each type of atom on both sides; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO balances.

misconceptions.question: In a half equation, which side do the electrons go?
misconceptions.correct: Electrons are lost at the positive electrode, so they are written on the right: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons can be added to whichever side makes the equation look balanced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'add electrons to balance the charge' is applied without asking which electrode it is.
misconceptions.correction: At the positive electrode negative ions lose electrons; the electrons appear as products.

misconceptions.question: Must the numbers of electrons match the charge?
misconceptions.correct: The number of electrons must balance the total charge, so two Br⁻ ions release two electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: One electron is enough however many ions react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charge on a single ion is copied without multiplying it.
misconceptions.correction: Charge must balance on both sides: 2Br⁻ carries 2−, so 2e⁻ must be released.

misconceptions.question: Are the substances in a mixture chemically combined?
misconceptions.correct: In a mixture the substances are not chemically combined together.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything mixed together has joined chemically.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday use of 'combine' means simply 'put together'.
misconceptions.correction: Chemical combination needs a reaction; stirring salt into water does not change either substance.

misconceptions.question: Do substances change their properties when mixed?
misconceptions.correct: The chemical properties of each substance in a mixture are unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Mixing changes what each substance is like.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mixtures often look different from their parts, so the substances seem changed.
misconceptions.correction: Iron filings mixed with sulfur are still attracted by a magnet; the iron is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Do separation techniques make new substances?
misconceptions.correct: Physical processes do not involve chemical reactions, so no new substances are made.
misconceptions.misconception: Distilling or filtering changes the substances involved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating is involved in distillation, and heating is associated with reactions.
misconceptions.correction: The substance collected after distillation is the same substance that boiled off.

misconceptions.question: Can filtration separate salt from salt solution?
misconceptions.correct: Filtration only separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; dissolved salt passes straight through the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: Filter paper removes anything that was added to the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filtering is described as 'cleaning' the liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Dissolved particles are far too small to be trapped; use crystallisation or distillation instead.

misconceptions.question: What does crystallisation leave behind?
misconceptions.correct: Crystallisation evaporates the solvent and leaves the dissolved solid as crystals.
misconceptions.misconception: The liquid is what you keep and the solid is lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Distillation, where the liquid is collected, is remembered instead.
misconceptions.correction: In crystallisation the solvent escapes as vapour and the solute stays in the dish.

misconceptions.question: What is collected in simple distillation of salt water?
misconceptions.correct: The water is boiled off, condensed and collected; the salt stays in the flask.
misconceptions.misconception: The salt travels over with the steam.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Separating salt water' is remembered without tracking which part moves.
misconceptions.correction: Salt has a very high boiling point, so only the water evaporates and condenses.

misconceptions.question: When is fractional distillation used?
misconceptions.correct: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids using the differences in their boiling points.
misconceptions.misconception: Fractional distillation is used to separate a dissolved solid from a liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both methods are called distillation, so the difference is lost.
misconceptions.correction: Use simple distillation for a solvent and a dissolved solid; use fractional distillation for two or more liquids.

misconceptions.question: How does paper chromatography separate a mixture?
misconceptions.correct: The substances separate because they move different distances with the solvent through the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: The heaviest or darkest substance always travels furthest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is the obvious feature of the spots, so it is assumed to control the result.
misconceptions.correction: How far a substance travels depends on how it is held by the paper and carried by the solvent, not on its colour.

misconceptions.question: Can an accepted scientific model be changed?
misconceptions.correct: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a model is accepted it is a proved fact and cannot change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Models are presented in textbooks as finished answers.
misconceptions.correction: The atomic model has been changed several times, each time because new evidence appeared.

misconceptions.question: What did scientists think atoms were before the electron was discovered?
misconceptions.correct: They were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms were already thought to have a nucleus and electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The modern picture is so familiar that it is assumed to have always existed.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus was only proposed after the alpha particle scattering results, long after the first sphere model.

misconceptions.question: What is the plum pudding model?
misconceptions.correct: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
misconceptions.misconception: A ball of negative charge with positive particles stuck in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charges are remembered as 'mixed up' without which is which.
misconceptions.correction: The dough is positive and the fruit is the negative electrons.

misconceptions.question: Does the plum pudding model have a nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: No. In the plum pudding model the positive charge is spread through the whole atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The plum pudding model has a small positive nucleus with electrons around it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every atom diagram met later has a nucleus, so one is added to this model too.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus is exactly what the plum pudding model lacked; that is why scattering results replaced it.

misconceptions.question: What did the alpha particle scattering results show?
misconceptions.correct: The mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and the nucleus is charged.
misconceptions.misconception: Because most particles went straight through, the atom must be solid throughout.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Most went straight through' is remembered without the few that were deflected.
misconceptions.correction: Most passing through shows the atom is mostly empty space; the few deflected back show a small, dense, charged centre.

misconceptions.question: Why were a few alpha particles deflected backwards?
misconceptions.correct: They came close to a small, dense, positively charged nucleus and were repelled.
misconceptions.misconception: The electrons in the atom pushed them back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrons are the particles most often talked about, so they are given the credit.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons have a very small mass and could not turn a fast alpha particle around; the nucleus did.

misconceptions.question: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model?
misconceptions.correct: He suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
misconceptions.misconception: He discovered the nucleus itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bohr's name is met alongside the nuclear model, so the discovery is attributed to him.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus came from the scattering results; Bohr adapted that model by fixing where the electrons orbit.

misconceptions.question: Did Bohr's ideas agree with experiments?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.
misconceptions.misconception: Bohr's model was only a guess with no support from observations.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Theoretical' is read as meaning unsupported.
misconceptions.correction: A theoretical model is accepted precisely because its calculations match what is measured.

misconceptions.question: Who or what showed that the nuclear charge is made of protons?
misconceptions.correct: Later experiments showed the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into whole numbers of identical particles, named protons.
misconceptions.misconception: James Chadwick discovered the proton.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chadwick is the only name attached to a sub-atomic particle in this topic.
misconceptions.correction: Chadwick's work provided evidence for the neutron; the proton came from earlier work on nuclear charge.

misconceptions.question: What did Chadwick's work provide evidence for?
misconceptions.correct: The existence of neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.
misconceptions.misconception: Chadwick found the electron.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The names of the scientists and the particles are learnt as a list and get paired wrongly.
misconceptions.correction: The electron was discovered before the plum pudding model; Chadwick's neutron came much later.

misconceptions.question: What are the relative charges of the three particles?
misconceptions.correct: Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1.
misconceptions.misconception: The neutron is not truly neutral; like the proton and electron it carries a small charge, so the three particle charges get muddled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Neutron' and 'negative' start with the same sound, and charges are recalled without a table.
misconceptions.correction: Neutral means no charge at all: the neutron's relative charge is 0.

misconceptions.question: Why does an atom have no overall charge?
misconceptions.correct: The number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the charges cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms are neutral because they contain neutrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'neutron' suggests it is what makes an atom neutral.
misconceptions.correction: Neutrons have no charge at all; it is the equal numbers of protons and electrons that cancel.

misconceptions.question: What does the atomic number tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The number of protons in an atom of that element.
misconceptions.misconception: The atomic number is the number of protons plus neutrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Atomic number and mass number are printed together and are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Atomic number counts protons only; the sum of protons and neutrons is the mass number.

misconceptions.question: Can two atoms of the same element have different numbers of protons?
misconceptions.correct: No. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms of an element may have different numbers of protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotopes are known to 'differ', and the difference is placed on the wrong particle.
misconceptions.correction: Isotopes of an element differ in neutrons; a change in protons makes it a different element.

misconceptions.question: How big is an atom?
misconceptions.correct: An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
misconceptions.misconception: An atom has a radius of about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The atom and nucleus figures are printed together and are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m is the size of the nucleus, ten thousand times smaller than the atom.

misconceptions.question: How does the nucleus compare in size with the atom?
misconceptions.correct: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus takes up a large part of the atom, about a tenth of its radius or even more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams draw the nucleus far too large because a true scale drawing is impossible.
misconceptions.correction: On a true scale, an atom the size of a sports stadium would have a nucleus the size of a pea.

misconceptions.question: Where is the mass of an atom?
misconceptions.correct: Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass is spread evenly through the atom, or the electrons carry much of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The nucleus looks tiny in diagrams, so it is assumed to be a small part of the mass.
misconceptions.correction: Protons and neutrons have a relative mass of 1 each; the electron's mass is very small.

misconceptions.question: What is the relative mass of an electron?
misconceptions.correct: Very small compared with a proton or a neutron.
misconceptions.misconception: An electron has the same mass as a proton but the opposite charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charges are equal and opposite, so the masses are assumed to match too.
misconceptions.correction: The charges are +1 and −1, but the electron's mass is negligible next to the proton's 1.

misconceptions.question: What is the mass number?
misconceptions.correct: The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number is the number of neutrons only.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Mass number minus atomic number gives neutrons' is remembered the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Mass number counts both particles in the nucleus; subtract the atomic number to find the neutrons.

misconceptions.question: How do isotopes of an element differ?
misconceptions.correct: They have different numbers of neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Isotopes have different numbers of electrons, or different numbers of protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any 'different atom of the same element' is assumed to differ in whatever particle is recalled first.
misconceptions.correction: Protons fix the element and electrons equal protons in an atom, so only the neutron number can vary.

misconceptions.question: Does an atom lose protons when it becomes a positive ion?
misconceptions.correct: No. It loses electrons; the number of protons never changes.
misconceptions.misconception: A 2+ charge means the atom has gained two protons or lost two protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charge is positive, so it is linked to the positive particle.
misconceptions.correction: Ions form by losing or gaining electrons; Mg²⁺ still has 12 protons but only 10 electrons.

misconceptions.question: What does relative atomic mass take account of?
misconceptions.correct: It is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the mass number of the most common isotope.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative atomic masses in the periodic table are often close to a whole number.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine is 35.5 because the average is weighted by how much of each isotope there is.

misconceptions.question: Is relative atomic mass the ordinary average of the isotope masses?
misconceptions.correct: No. Each isotope mass is weighted by its abundance before averaging.
misconceptions.misconception: Add the isotope mass numbers and divide by how many isotopes there are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'average' is taken to mean the mean learnt in maths.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance, add these, then divide by 100.

misconceptions.question: Which energy level do electrons fill first?
misconceptions.correct: The lowest available energy level (the innermost available shell).
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons fill the outer shell first, or spread themselves evenly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reactions involve outer electrons, so the outer shell seems to be filled first.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, so the first shell fills before the second.

misconceptions.question: What does the electronic structure 2,8,1 mean?
misconceptions.correct: Two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second and one in the third.
misconceptions.misconception: The numbers count the shells, or they are written outermost first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The list is read without checking which end is the innermost shell.
misconceptions.correction: Read from the left, starting at the shell nearest the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What are the products when a metal reacts with an acid?
misconceptions.correct: A salt and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal and an acid react to give a salt and water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutralisation of an alkali by an acid gives a salt and water, and the two cases are merged.
misconceptions.correction: Test for the gas: a metal and an acid always release hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop.

misconceptions.question: Which part of a filtered mixture is the residue?
misconceptions.correct: The insoluble solid left on the filter paper is the residue; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
misconceptions.misconception: The liquid caught in the paper is what has been separated out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two new words are met together and are easily exchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the liquid: it goes through the paper into the beaker, so only solid can stay behind.

misconceptions.question: What makes scientists change a model?
misconceptions.correct: New experimental evidence that the old model cannot explain.
misconceptions.misconception: A model changes because a scientist prefers a different idea.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Model changes are told as stories about individuals, so the evidence gets left out.
misconceptions.correction: Each change to the atomic model followed a result that the previous model could not explain.

misconceptions.question: How big is a nanometre?
misconceptions.correct: A nanometre is 1 x 10⁻⁹ m, a million times smaller than a millimetre.
misconceptions.misconception: A nanometre is about the same as a millimetre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are small units written with the metre symbol, so they are treated as similar.
misconceptions.correction: An atomic radius of 0.1 nm is 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m, far smaller than anything visible.

misconceptions.question: How many electrons fit in the first two energy levels?
misconceptions.correct: Two in the first energy level and eight in the second.
misconceptions.misconception: Eight electrons fit in the first energy level.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'eight' of the second shell is remembered and applied to the first.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium is 2,8,1: two in the first level, eight in the second, one in the third.

misconceptions.question: (HT only) Which ions are written in an ionic equation?
misconceptions.correct: Only the ions and atoms that take part in the reaction; spectator ions are left out.
misconceptions.misconception: Every ion from the full equation must still appear in the ionic equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing rules say nothing may be added or taken away, so leaving ions out looks like breaking the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Cross out any ion that is the same on both sides; what is left is the ionic equation.

misconceptions.question: A student evaporates the water from an ink containing several dissolved dyes. Are the dyes now separated from each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Crystallisation only separates dissolved solids from the solvent; the dyes are left behind still mixed together, so chromatography is needed to separate them.
misconceptions.misconception: Crystallising or evaporating a solution separates the dissolved substances from one another, not just from the solvent.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crystallisation is taught as a separation technique, so students overgeneralise it to any mixture, not noticing it only splits solute from solvent.
misconceptions.correction: Crystallisation removes the solvent, leaving all the solutes mixed in the solid residue. To separate several substances dissolved in the same solvent, such as the dyes in ink, paper chromatography is used.

misconceptions.question: An atom is written with mass number 23 and atomic number 11. Which number gives the number of protons?
misconceptions.correct: The atomic number, 11, gives the number of protons; the mass number, 23, is protons plus neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number gives the number of protons and the atomic number gives the number of neutrons, so the two numbers are swapped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two unfamiliar numbers are met at once, and 'mass' suggests it counts the important heavy protons, so students attach the larger number to protons.
misconceptions.correction: Protons = atomic number; neutrons = mass number minus atomic number; electrons equal protons in a neutral atom. For chlorine-35 this gives 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes what an atom is?

options.text: The smallest part of an element that can exist
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of an atom.

options.text: The smallest particle that can ever exist
options.rationale: Drops 'of an element'; protons, neutrons and electrons are smaller than an atom.

options.text: The smallest part of any compound that exists
options.rationale: Describes a particle of a compound, not an atom of an element.

options.text: A particle made of two or more atoms joined
options.rationale: This describes a molecule, which is built from atoms.

mcqs.stem: Which option gives the chemical symbols correctly?

options.text: So is sodium and Ox is oxygen
options.rationale: Invents symbols from the first two letters of the English names.

options.text: Na is sodium and O is oxygen
options.rationale: Na represents an atom of sodium and O an atom of oxygen.

options.text: N is sodium and O is oxygen
options.rationale: N is the symbol for nitrogen, not for sodium.

options.text: Na is sodium, O2 is oxygen
options.rationale: O2 is a formula for an oxygen molecule, not the symbol for an atom.

mcqs.stem: About how many different elements are there, and where are they shown?

options.text: About 100 elements and compounds, shown in the table
options.rationale: The periodic table shows elements only, never compounds.

options.text: About 20 elements only, all shown in the periodic table
options.rationale: Only the first 20 elements are learnt in detail; about 100 exist.

options.text: About 100 elements, all shown in the periodic table
options.rationale: Matches the specification: about 100 elements, shown in the periodic table.

options.text: Many thousands of elements, most not in the table
options.rationale: There are many thousands of compounds, but only about 100 elements.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a compound is correct?

options.text: Its elements can be mixed together in any proportions at all
options.rationale: Any proportion describes a mixture; a compound has a fixed formula.

options.text: Its elements keep all the properties they had before mixing
options.rationale: Substances keep their properties in a mixture, not in a compound.

options.text: Its elements can be separated from it by simple filtration
options.rationale: Filtration is a physical process and cannot split a compound.

options.text: Its elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions
options.rationale: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.

mcqs.stem: What must happen in every chemical reaction?

options.text: A detectable energy change must be measured
options.rationale: The specification says reactions often, not always, involve a detectable energy change.

options.text: One or more new substances must always be formed
options.rationale: Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances.

options.text: A gas or a change of colour must be seen
options.rationale: Many reactions show no visible change at all.

options.text: Two elements must join to make a compound
options.rationale: Some reactions break compounds up rather than build them.

mcqs.stem: How can a compound be separated into its elements?

options.text: Only by using a chemical reaction
options.rationale: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.

options.text: By filtering it through filter paper
options.rationale: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid in a mixture.

options.text: By evaporating the liquid away from it
options.rationale: Evaporation is a physical process and makes no new substances.

options.text: By distilling the compound in a flask
options.rationale: Distillation separates mixtures; it cannot break chemical bonds.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Which is the correct word equation?

options.text: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water
options.rationale: A metal and an acid give a salt and hydrogen, not water.

options.text: Mg + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
options.rationale: A word equation must use names throughout, not the symbol Mg.

options.text: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
options.rationale: Reactant names on the left, product names on the right, all written as words.

options.text: magnesium + HCl → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
options.rationale: Mixing the chemical formula HCl into an otherwise word equation is exactly m13 (symbols or formulae mixed into a word equation). Stays a plausible wrong answer; length 47, distinct from 58, 54, 61.

mcqs.stem: A compound has the formula MgO. What is its name?

options.text: Magnesium oxygen
options.rationale: The second element's name must change to end in -ide.

options.text: Magnesium oxide
options.rationale: The metal keeps its name and oxygen becomes oxide.

options.text: Magnesium dioxide
options.rationale: There is only one oxygen atom, and no prefix is used here.

options.text: Magnesium monoxide
options.rationale: Adding a prefix to the oxide (mono-, by analogy with carbon monoxide) for the single-atom MgO is m15 (a prefix should be added whenever a formula has more than one atom). Plausible wrong answer; length 18, distinct from 16, 15, 17.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which symbol equation represents this reaction correctly?

options.text: Mg + O₂ → MgO
options.rationale: Two oxygen atoms on the left but only one on the right.

options.text: Mg + O₂ → MgO₂
options.rationale: Balances by changing the formula, which invents a new substance.

options.text: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
options.rationale: Two Mg atoms and two O atoms on each side, with the products on the right.

options.text: 2Mg + 2O₂ → 2MgO
options.rationale: There are now four oxygen atoms on the left but only two on the right.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows what happens at the positive electrode?

options.text: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
options.rationale: The charge does not balance: two Br⁻ ions must release two electrons.

options.text: Br⁻ + e⁻ → Br₂
options.rationale: Electrons are lost at the positive electrode, not gained.

options.text: Br⁻ + Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
options.rationale: Two bromide ions react but only one electron is released (should be 2e⁻) - exactly m20 (one electron is enough however many ions react). Correctly forms Br₂, so it stays a plausible wrong half-equation; length 20, distinct from 15, 14, 16.

options.text: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: Two bromide ions lose two electrons and form a bromine molecule.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a mixture?

options.text: Two or more substances that are chemically combined
options.rationale: Chemical combination gives a compound, not a mixture.

options.text: Two substances whose properties have both changed
options.rationale: The chemical properties of each substance in a mixture are unchanged.

options.text: Two or more substances not chemically combined
options.rationale: A mixture consists of elements or compounds not chemically combined together.

options.text: Two elements joined in fixed proportions by mass
options.rationale: Fixed proportions describe a compound.

mcqs.stem: A mixture of ethanol and water is separated by fractional distillation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: New substances are made because the mixture has been heated up
options.rationale: Heating a mixture to separate it does not make new substances.

options.text: The ethanol collected has different properties from before
options.rationale: The ethanol is unchanged by being separated.

options.text: The two liquids react with each other as they are heated
options.rationale: Ethanol and water in a mixture are not chemically combined.

options.text: No new substances are made, as no chemical reaction happens
options.rationale: Separation methods are physical processes, so no new substances are made.

mcqs.stem: Sand is stirred into salty water and the mixture is filtered. What is left on the filter paper?

options.text: The sand only, because it does not dissolve
options.rationale: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, so the sand is the residue.

options.text: The sand and the salt, which are both solids
options.rationale: Dissolved salt passes through the filter paper with the water.

options.text: The salty water, which stays in the paper
options.rationale: The liquid that passes through is the filtrate, not the residue.

options.text: The salt, as filtering removes dissolved solids
options.rationale: Believing the filter paper traps the dissolved salt is m24 (filter paper removes anything that was added to the water). Plausible wrong answer; length 47, distinct from 43, 44, 41.

mcqs.stem: Copper sulfate solution is left in an evaporating basin until crystals form. What has happened?

options.text: The copper sulfate evaporated, leaving the water behind
options.rationale: The dissolved solid stays behind; it is the solvent that evaporates.

options.text: The water has evaporated, leaving the copper sulfate
options.rationale: In crystallisation the solvent evaporates and the solute is left as crystals.

options.text: The copper sulfate has reacted to make a blue solid
options.rationale: Crystallisation is a physical process, so no new substance is made.

options.text: The water was condensed on a lid and collected
options.rationale: That describes distillation, in which the solvent is collected.

mcqs.stem: Sea water is separated by simple distillation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Salt boils off, then condenses and is collected
options.rationale: Salt has a very high boiling point and does not evaporate here.

options.text: Both parts boil off at different temperatures
options.rationale: That describes fractional distillation of two liquids.

options.text: The salt evaporates and is lost, leaving the water
options.rationale: Thinking the salt (solid) boils/evaporates off and is lost while the water (liquid) is kept is m25 (the liquid is what you keep and the solid is lost). Plausible wrong distillation answer; length 50, distinct from 47, 45, 43.

options.text: Water boils off, condenses and is collected
options.rationale: The solvent evaporates, is condensed and collected, and the salt stays behind.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to find out how many coloured dyes are in a sample of ink. Which technique should be used?

options.text: Filtration using filter paper and a glass funnel
options.rationale: The dyes are dissolved, so they pass straight through the filter paper.

options.text: Fractional distillation of the ink sample
options.rationale: Fractional distillation separates liquids by boiling point, not dissolved dyes.

options.text: Paper chromatography with a suitable solvent
options.rationale: Chromatography separates the dyes by how far each one moves with the solvent.

options.text: Crystallisation in an evaporating basin
options.rationale: This would leave a mixed solid, showing nothing about the dyes.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about scientific models is correct?

options.text: New experimental evidence may lead to a model being replaced
options.rationale: This is the specification statement about how scientific models change.

options.text: Once a model has been accepted it can no longer be changed
options.rationale: The atomic model has been changed several times.

options.text: A model changes when a scientist prefers a different idea
options.rationale: Models change in response to evidence, not to personal preference.

options.text: A model that explains most results is never questioned
options.rationale: The plum pudding model explained a great deal and was still replaced.

mcqs.stem: What were atoms thought to be like before the electron was discovered?

options.text: Tiny spheres with a nucleus in the middle
options.rationale: The nucleus was only proposed after the alpha particle scattering experiment.

options.text: Balls of negative charge holding protons
options.rationale: This reverses the charges of the plum pudding model, which came later.

options.text: Spheres with electrons in set orbits
options.rationale: Orbits at specific distances were suggested by Bohr much later.

options.text: Tiny spheres that could not be divided
options.rationale: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be indivisible spheres.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the plum pudding model of the atom?

options.text: A ball of negative charge with positive particles inside it
options.rationale: The charges are the wrong way round.

options.text: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of the plum pudding model.

options.text: A small positive nucleus with electrons around the outside
options.rationale: That is the nuclear model, which replaced the plum pudding model.

options.text: A solid sphere of matter that cannot be divided at all
options.rationale: That is the model used before the electron was discovered.

mcqs.stem: What conclusion came from the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment?

options.text: The positive charge is spread evenly through the whole atom
options.rationale: That is the plum pudding model, which these results replaced.

options.text: The atom is a solid ball of matter with no gaps in it
options.rationale: Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space.

options.text: Electrons in the atom deflect the alpha particles back
options.rationale: Electrons are far too light to deflect an alpha particle backwards.

options.text: The mass of an atom is concentrated at a charged centre
options.rationale: The results led to the conclusion that the mass is concentrated at a charged nucleus.

mcqs.stem: In the scattering experiment a few alpha particles were deflected straight back. Why did this change the atomic model?

options.text: It showed that the whole atom is filled with positive charge
options.rationale: A large deflection shows the charge is concentrated, not spread out.

options.text: It showed that electrons are far heavier than was thought
options.rationale: The deflection is caused by the nucleus, not by the electrons.

options.text: The plum pudding model could not explain such large deflections
options.rationale: A spread-out positive charge could not turn a fast alpha particle around.

options.text: It proved that atoms are tiny spheres that cannot be split
options.rationale: That model had already been replaced when the electron was discovered.

mcqs.stem: What is the main difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?

options.text: In the nuclear model the mass and charge are in the nucleus
options.rationale: The nuclear model concentrates the mass and the positive charge at the centre.

options.text: In the plum pudding model the electrons orbit a small nucleus
options.rationale: The plum pudding model has no nucleus at all.

options.text: In the nuclear model the electrons are embedded in positive charge
options.rationale: That describes the plum pudding model.

options.text: In the nuclear model the mass is spread evenly through the atom
options.rationale: Almost all of the mass is in the nucleus in the nuclear model.

mcqs.stem: What did Niels Bohr suggest, and how did his idea compare with experiment?

options.text: Electrons orbit at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with observations
options.rationale: Bohr adapted the nuclear model, and his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.

options.text: Electrons orbit at specific distances, but no experimental observations supported this
options.rationale: Bohr's calculations did agree with experimental observations.

options.text: The nucleus exists, and his calculations agreed with the observations
options.rationale: The nucleus came from the scattering results, not from Bohr.

options.text: Electrons deflect the alpha particles, and this matched results
options.rationale: Mis-attributing the scattering deflection-by-electrons idea to Bohr is m34 (the electrons in the atom pushed the alpha particles back); students routinely conflate the scattering work with Bohr. Plausible wrong answer; length 63, distinct from 84, 86, 69.

mcqs.stem: What did later experiments show about the positive charge of a nucleus?

options.text: It can be divided into whole numbers of identical charges
options.rationale: Each of these identical smaller charges was named a proton.

options.text: It is carried by one single particle found by James Chadwick
options.rationale: Chadwick's work provided the evidence for the neutron.

options.text: It comes from the neutrons, which each carry a small charge
options.rationale: Neutrons have no charge at all.

options.text: It is spread evenly through the atom, not in a nucleus
options.rationale: That is the plum pudding model, which had already been replaced.

mcqs.stem: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?

options.text: Protons inside the nucleus, about 20 years after this was accepted
options.rationale: Protons were named from earlier work on the charge of the nucleus.

options.text: Neutrons inside the nucleus, about 20 years after it was accepted
options.rationale: Chadwick's work showed that neutrons exist within the nucleus.

options.text: Electrons, which had been found long before the nuclear model
options.rationale: The electron was discovered before the plum pudding model.

options.text: The nucleus itself, at the centre of every atom
options.rationale: Crediting Chadwick with discovering the nucleus is m35 (he discovered the nucleus itself). Plausible scientist-confusion wrong answer for a neutron question; length 47, distinct from 66, 65, 61.

mcqs.stem: What are the relative electrical charges of a proton, a neutron and an electron?

options.text: Proton and neutron +1, electron −1
options.rationale: The neutron has no charge; it is its relative mass, not its charge, that is 1.

options.text: Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
options.rationale: These are the relative electrical charges given in the specification.

options.text: Proton 0, neutron +1 and electron −1
options.rationale: The proton is the positively charged particle in the nucleus.

options.text: Every particle has a charge of +1 or −1
options.rationale: Neutral means no charge, so the neutron is 0.

mcqs.stem: An atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does it have, and why?

options.text: 0, because neutrons make the atom neutral overall
options.rationale: Neutrons have no charge; the balance comes from protons and electrons.

options.text: 23, because protons and neutrons are added together
options.rationale: Using protons+neutrons (the mass number, 23 for sodium) as the electron count applies m41's characteristic protons-plus-neutrons sum. Plausible wrong answer; length 50, distinct from 49, 39, 53.

options.text: 10, because it loses one of its protons
options.rationale: m49 (charge is due to gaining/losing protons) conflates protons and electrons, so the student subtracts a proton and reports 10. Plausible wrong answer; length 39, distinct from 49, 50, 53.

options.text: 11, because electrons and protons are equal in number
options.rationale: In an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

mcqs.stem: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?

options.text: The total of the protons and neutrons
options.rationale: That total is the mass number.

options.text: The number of protons in each atom
options.rationale: The number of protons in an atom of an element is its atomic number.

options.text: The number of neutrons inside each atom
options.rationale: Neutrons are found by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number.

options.text: The number of electrons per shell
options.rationale: Reading the atomic number as if it stated the per-shell electron arrangement is m53 (the notation numbers are misread). Plausible wrong answer; length 33, distinct from 37, 34, 39.

mcqs.stem: Two atoms each have 6 protons but different masses. What must be true?

options.text: They are atoms of different elements
options.rationale: A different element would have a different number of protons.

options.text: They must have different numbers of electrons
options.rationale: m48 (isotopes have different numbers of electrons) directly generates the claim that the two atoms differ in electrons. Plausible wrong answer; length 45, distinct from 36, 34, 43.

options.text: They are atoms of the same element
options.rationale: All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.

options.text: They must have different numbers of protons
options.rationale: m42 (atoms of an element may have different numbers of protons) makes the student infer that a mass difference means a proton difference. Plausible wrong answer; length 43, distinct from 36, 45, 34.

mcqs.stem: What is the approximate radius of an atom?

options.rationale: A millimetre is a million times larger than a nanometre.
This is between the size of an atom and the size of a nucleus.

options.text: 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m)
options.rationale: This is the value given in the specification.
This is far smaller than an atom, though still larger than a nucleus.

mcqs.stem: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?

options.text: Less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom
options.rationale: The specification gives less than 1/10 000, about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m.

options.text: About 1/10 of the radius of the whole atom
options.rationale: Diagrams exaggerate the nucleus; it is far smaller than this.

options.text: About the same as the radius of the atom
options.rationale: The nucleus is a tiny part of the atom.

options.text: About half the radius of the whole atom
options.rationale: This would leave almost no space for the electrons.

mcqs.stem: An atom is imagined to be as wide as a sports stadium. On this scale, about how large is the nucleus?

options.text: About the size of the whole football pitch
options.rationale: That would make the nucleus roughly a tenth of the atom.

options.text: About the size of one of the stands
options.rationale: Still thousands of times too large.

options.text: About the size of a pea in the middle
options.rationale: The nucleus radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's, so it is minute on this scale.

options.text: About the size of half the stadium
options.rationale: That would leave no room for the electrons.

mcqs.stem: Why is almost all of the mass of an atom in the nucleus?

options.text: The nucleus takes up nearly all of the atom's volume
options.rationale: The nucleus radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius.

options.text: Protons and electrons have equal masses but opposite charges
options.rationale: Only the charges are equal and opposite; the electron's mass is very small.

options.text: Only neutrons in the nucleus have any mass at all
options.rationale: Protons have a relative mass of 1 as well.

options.text: Protons and neutrons have a relative mass of 1 each
options.rationale: The nucleus holds all the protons and neutrons, which carry the mass.

mcqs.stem: What are the relative masses of a proton, a neutron and an electron?

options.text: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small
options.rationale: These are the relative masses given in the specification.

options.text: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron also 1
options.rationale: The electron's relative mass is very small, not 1.

options.text: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron 1 but negative
options.rationale: Giving the electron a mass of 1 with the opposite (negative) charge is exactly m46 (an electron has the same mass as a proton but the opposite charge). Plausible wrong answer, distinct in emphasis from the sibling; length 44, distinct from 40, 36, 43.

options.text: Proton 1, neutron very small and electron 1
options.rationale: The neutron has a relative mass of 1, like the proton.

mcqs.stem: What is the mass number of an atom?

options.text: The sum of its protons and electrons
options.rationale: Electrons have almost no mass and are not counted.

options.text: The sum of its protons and neutrons
options.rationale: The specification defines the mass number as the sum of the protons and neutrons.

options.text: The number of protons that it contains
options.rationale: That is the atomic number.

options.text: The number of neutrons it contains
options.rationale: Neutrons alone give the mass number minus the atomic number.

mcqs.stem: What are isotopes?

options.text: Atoms of the same element but with different numbers of protons
options.rationale: Changing the number of protons changes the element.

options.text: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons
options.rationale: An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

options.text: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of isotopes.

options.text: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
options.rationale: Isotopes are always atoms of one element.

mcqs.stem: A chlorine atom is written with mass number 35 and atomic number 17. What does it contain?

options.text: 17 protons, 35 neutrons, plus 17 electrons
options.rationale: 35 is the mass number, not the number of neutrons.

options.text: 35 protons, with 17 neutrons and 35 electrons
options.rationale: The atomic number, 17, gives the number of protons.

options.text: 9 protons, 8 neutrons and 9 electrons
options.rationale: The protons and neutrons have been swapped over.

options.text: 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons
options.rationale: Protons = 17, neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18, and electrons equal protons.

mcqs.stem: A chloride ion is written Cl⁻. A chlorine atom has atomic number 17. Which is correct for the ion?

options.text: 16 protons and 17 electrons, one proton lost
options.rationale: Believing the minus charge means a proton was lost is m49 (charge comes from gaining/losing protons), giving 16 protons. Plausible wrong answer; length 44, distinct from 48, 47, 45.

options.text: 18 protons and 18 electrons, since it is neutral
options.rationale: The number of protons never changes when an ion forms.

options.text: 17 protons and 17 electrons, as they stay equal
options.rationale: Equal numbers would mean no overall charge.

options.text: 17 protons and 18 electrons, as one is gained
options.rationale: The 1− charge shows one extra electron; the number of protons is unchanged.

mcqs.stem: What does the relative atomic mass of an element take account of?

options.text: The abundance of each of its isotopes
options.rationale: Relative atomic mass is an average that takes account of isotope abundance.

options.text: The mass number of its commonest isotope
options.rationale: That ignores the other isotopes completely.

options.text: The average of its isotope mass numbers
options.rationale: The average must be weighted by the abundance of each isotope.

options.text: The number of protons and neutrons combined
options.rationale: Equating relative atomic mass with the protons-plus-neutrons total applies m41's characteristic sum (confusing it with the mass number). Plausible wrong answer; length 43, distinct from 37, 40, 39.

mcqs.stem: Lithium has two isotopes: 7.5% is ⁶Li and 92.5% is ⁷Li. What is the relative atomic mass of lithium?

options.rationale: This is the simple mean of 6 and 7, ignoring the abundances.
This uses only the most abundant isotope.
This adds the two mass numbers instead of averaging them.

mcqs.stem: In which order do electrons occupy the energy levels (shells) of an atom?

options.text: The outer shell is filled before the inner ones
options.rationale: Reactions involve outer electrons, but filling starts at the centre.

options.text: They spread out evenly between the shells
options.rationale: Each level is filled in turn before the next one is used.

options.text: The lowest available energy level is filled first
options.rationale: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, the innermost available shells.

options.text: The first shell takes eight electrons first
options.rationale: The first energy level holds only two electrons.

mcqs.stem: A magnesium atom has 12 electrons. Which electronic structure is correct?

options.rationale: Both of the last two electrons fit in the third energy level.

Filling the first shell to eight (then 4 remaining) for magnesium's 12 electrons is exactly m54 (eight electrons fit in the first energy level). Plausible wrong answer; length 3, distinct from 7, 1, 5.
Writing the number of shells (3) as the structure is m53 (the notation numbers count the shells). Plausible wrong answer; length 1, distinct from 7, 3, 5.
Two electrons fill the first level and eight the second, leaving two in the third.

mcqs.stem: The electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1. What does the final 1 tell you?

options.text: There is one electron in the third energy level
options.rationale: The numbers are read outwards, so the last one is the outermost level.

options.text: There is one electron in the innermost shell only
options.rationale: The first number, 2, gives the lowest energy level.

options.text: One of the shells in the atom is completely full
options.rationale: The numbers count the electrons in each level, not the full shells.

options.text: The last shell was filled up first of all
options.rationale: Reading the final 1 as the outer shell being filled before the inner ones is m52 (electrons fill the outer shell first). Plausible wrong answer; length 41, distinct from 47, 49, 48.

mcqs.stem: Why is the electronic structure of sodium 2,8,1 rather than 2,9?

options.text: The first energy level always holds eight electrons
options.rationale: Believing the first level holds eight electrons is exactly m54 (eight electrons fit in the first energy level), which would wrongly account for 2,8,1. Plausible wrong answer; length 51, distinct from 50, 55, 57.

options.text: The second energy level holds only eight electrons
options.rationale: Once the second level holds eight, the next electron starts the third level.

options.text: The outer energy level is always filled up first of all
options.rationale: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy level first.

options.text: The numbers are read from the outside of the atom inwards
options.rationale: The numbers are read from the innermost energy level outwards.

mcqs.stem: A fluorine atom has 9 electrons. Which shell diagram is correct?

options.text: 2 on the first ring and 7 on the second
options.rationale: The first energy level is full with two electrons, so the other seven go in the second.

options.text: 8 on the first ring and 1 on the second
options.rationale: The first energy level holds only two electrons; eight belongs to the second.

options.text: 7 on the first ring and 2 on the second
options.rationale: This draws the rings outermost first; the innermost ring is filled first.

options.text: 5 on the first ring and 4 on the second
options.rationale: Electrons do not spread out evenly; the lowest level fills before the next.

mcqs.stem: A shell diagram is drawn with 4 electrons on the outer ring, 8 on the middle ring and 2 on the inner ring. Which electronic structure does it show?

options.rationale: The structure starts at the innermost ring: 2, then 8, then 4.
This lists the rings from the outside in; the innermost ring is written first.
The first energy level holds two electrons, not eight.
Electrons fill the lowest level first rather than spreading out evenly.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) Silver nitrate solution reacts with sodium chloride solution: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq). Which is the correct ionic equation?

options.text: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
options.rationale: Only these ions change; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions and are left out.

options.text: Ag⁺(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)
options.rationale: Sodium chloride solution is already separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

options.text: AgNO₃(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
options.rationale: Silver nitrate solution is already separate Ag⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions.

options.text: Na⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) → NaNO₃(aq)
options.rationale: These are the spectator ions, unchanged by the reaction.

mcqs.stem: Ink is spotted on chromatography paper and a solvent runs up it. Why do the dyes separate?

options.text: They move different distances with the solvent
options.rationale: Each dye is held by the paper and carried by the solvent to a different extent.

options.text: The darkest dye always travels the furthest
options.rationale: How far a dye travels does not depend on its colour.

options.text: The paper traps each dye as a filter would
options.rationale: Dissolved dyes are far too small to be trapped by the paper.

options.text: The paper reacts with the dyes to make new ones
options.rationale: Chromatography is a physical process, so no new substances are made.

mcqs.stem: A mixture of ethanol and water is separated by fractional distillation. Why does this method work?

options.text: The two liquids boil at different temperatures
options.rationale: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids using their different boiling points.

options.text: One is a solid dissolved in the other liquid
options.rationale: Ethanol and water are both liquids; a dissolved solid needs simple distillation.

options.text: Heating the mixture makes new substances form
options.rationale: No chemical reaction happens, so no new substances are made.

options.text: Water evaporates away, leaving the ethanol
options.rationale: That describes crystallisation; here both liquids boil and each is collected.
